title: Hands open at the end (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 5:14)
hook: we are born with fists closed and leave with hands open
tomorrow: no one leaves with even half of what they wanted. is that bad news?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king's son too far from home, and a father who said: come as far as you're able. I'll come the rest. Today the week comes back, and it turns out to be about hands.
screen: `I'LL COME THE REST.` → `A WEEK ABOUT HANDS.`

segments.voice: Hold a newborn and offer a finger, and the tiny hand often curls around it and won't let go. It feels like being chosen. A newborn's hands are often closed into fists. Ecclesiastes Rabbah, a midrash on the book of Kohelet, looks at those fists and reads a whole life in them. And at the other end of life, it looks at the hands again.
screen: `A TINY HAND, HOLDING ON.` → `A WHOLE LIFE IN A FIST.` → `THEN, THE HANDS AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Kohelet says it plainly: "As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he go back as he came." The midrash adds the hands. A person comes into the world with fists closed, as if to say: the whole world is mine, I'll take it all. And leaves with hands spread open, as if to say: I've taken nothing from this world. It isn't telling anyone to stop holding things. An open hand can still carry a cup, or another hand. It just can't grip. Tradition says Kohelet was King Solomon, and the book itself says its author gathered silver and gold; he is the one who notices that it all stays behind. A parent could use this when a child asks why we can't keep things forever. Now look back at the week, and it's a week of loosening fingers. One boat: the seat isn't only yours. Care for the image: even your body is held in trust. Great is peace: let a wounding word drop. Go to each side: walk over and sit down. A needle's eye: open just a little. I'll come the rest: you don't have to carry the whole road. Six ways of opening a hand before the end asks you to.
screen: `NAKED HE GOES BACK.` · `FISTS: THE WORLD IS MINE.` · `OPEN: I TOOK NOTHING.` · `A WEEK OF LOOSENING FINGERS.` · then, large: `HANDS OPEN AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Make two fists in your lap and hold them tight for a few breaths, noticing how much effort gripping takes. Then let them fall open, palms up, and leave them that way for the rest of the sit. Each time your fingers start to curl again, let them open.
screen: `TWO FISTS, HELD TIGHT.` · `LET THEM FALL OPEN.` · `PALMS UP TILL THE BELL.`

segments.voice: Hands open at the end: Ecclesiastes Rabbah's picture of a life. Born with fists closed, as if the world is ours; leaving with hands open, taking nothing.
screen: `HANDS OPEN AT THE END — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hands open at the end. An open hand can still hold a lot; it just doesn't grip.

howItsDone: Jews read Kohelet, Ecclesiastes, in synagogue on Sukkot in many communities, and its midrash, Ecclesiastes Rabbah, is studied for its teachings on wanting, owning and letting go.

fork.setup: your grandmother is moving somewhere smaller and has to give away things she loves. she asks for your help, and she's sad. by the midrash, what helps most?

fork.reveal: the midrash pictures a life that ends with open hands. opening them toward people she loves is letting go without losing what mattered.
